Zinc Framework Concepts

Architecture

Zinc is designed with performance and simplicity in mind. Its architecture follows a clean, modular approach with components that work together efficiently.

Router Internals

The router is the core component of Zinc, responsible for matching incoming HTTP requests to the appropriate handlers. Understanding its internal design helps to grasp how Zinc achieves its high performance.

Route Tree Structure

Zinc uses a tree-based structure for routing, which provides O(log n) lookup times:

  • Each route is represented as a node in a prefix tree (trie)
  • Path segments are used as edges between nodes
  • Special handling exists for parameter segments (starting with ':') and wildcards ('*')
  • Handlers are attached to leaf nodes or nodes with methods

The RouteNode structure represents nodes in this tree: 


type RouteNode struct {
    path     string
    part     string
    children []*RouteNode
    handler  RouteHandler
    handlers map[string]RouteHandler // Map of handlers by method
    isParam  bool
    isWild   bool
    method   string
}

Route Registration

When you register a route using app.Get(), app.Post(), etc., Zinc performs these steps:

  1. Normalizes the path (handles trailing slashes, etc.)
  2. Breaks the path into segments
  3. Traverses the route tree, creating nodes as needed
  4. Attaches the handler to the final node with the appropriate HTTP method

Path parameters and wildcards are detected during this process and marked in the tree.

Request Routing

When a request arrives, Zinc:

  1. First checks for direct static route matches (fast path)
  2. If not found, checks the route cache for common dynamic routes
  3. If still not found, traverses the route tree to find a matching handler
  4. Extracts path parameters during traversal
  5. Stores matched routes in the cache for future requests

Route Caching

Zinc includes an efficient route cache system that significantly improves performance: 


type RouteCache struct {
    cache map[routeCacheKey]routeCacheEntry
    mu    sync.RWMutex
    size  int
}

type routeCacheKey struct {
    method string
    path   string
}

type routeCacheEntry struct {
    handler RouteHandler
    context *Context
}

The cache avoids expensive tree traversals for frequently accessed routes, particularly dynamic routes with parameters.

Path Parameter Handling

Path parameters (e.g., /users/:id) are handled efficiently:

  • Parameters are detected during route registration
  • Values are extracted during request routing
  • Parameters are stored in a fixed-size array (params) to avoid allocations
  • The Context provides access to these parameters via c.Param("name")

type param struct {
    key   string
    value string
}

type params [4]param  // Fixed-size array for common use cases

Memory Optimization

Zinc employs several memory optimization strategies:

  • Context pooling to reduce garbage collection pressure
  • Fixed-size arrays for common operations
  • Path segment caching with sync.Pool
  • Pre-allocation of common data structures

var contextPool = sync.Pool{
    New: func() interface{} {
        // Pre-allocate with fixed-size maps to avoid dynamic resizing
        c := &Context{
            Store:    make(map[string]interface{}, 4),
            services: make(map[string]interface{}, 4),
            status:   http.StatusOK,
            index:    -1,
        }
        return c
    },
}

Middleware Chain

Middleware in Zinc follows a chain-of-responsibility pattern:

  • Middleware functions are chained together in a specific order
  • Each middleware can execute code before and after the next middleware
  • The Context's Next() method controls flow through the chain
  • Middleware can be applied at app, group, or route level

The middleware execution flow can be visualized as a nested onion-like structure, where each layer can perform operations before and after the inner layers.

Performance Considerations

Zinc is designed for high performance, with several optimizations:

  • Fast path for static routes
  • Route caching for dynamic routes
  • Memory pooling to reduce garbage collection
  • Efficient path parameter extraction
  • Minimized allocations during request handling
  • Fixed-size data structures where appropriate

These optimizations allow Zinc to handle a high number of requests with minimal latency and resource usage, making it suitable for high-performance API servers.
